newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia fuel oil to rise on S.Korea,Kuwait export cut.
newsitem.headline: Asia fuel oil to rise on S.Korea,Kuwait export cut.

text.p: Asian fuel oil prices are poised to soar on projections of lower exports from South Korea and Kuwait, as well as strong demand from China, the region's main importer, industry sources said on Thursday.
Kuwait is expected to half its exports starting in May, while South Korean exports would also be cut by nearly a quarter. South Korea exports around 600,000 tonnes of fuel oil every month.
"Kuwait is exporting only two cargoes in May, compared to four in April," a trader familiar with Kuwaiti exports said.
Traders attributed the reduced exports to rising fuel oil demand for air-conditioning as summer approaches and the ongoing maintenance works at Kuwait's biggest refinery.
Maintenance work at the 420,000-barrel-per-day (bpd) Mina Al-Ahmadi refinery began in March and was expected to be completed by end-April.
Exports from Bahrain might also be reduced as a secondary processing unit at the 250,000-bpd refinery in Sitra undergoes maintenance in April, traders said.
But Iran is still exporting its usual four 80,000-tonne cargoes of fuel oil every month, they said.

Traders said while poor bunker fuel demand in Fujairah, in the United Arab Emirates, has prompted two oil trading companies to move more than 80,000 tonnes to Singapore, the excess cargoes would be easily absorb.

"Yes, the market in the near term or the next two to three weeks may still be depressed but prices should rise in the second half of May when Asia's refinery shutdown season begins," a trader with a European firm said.
Refinery shutdowns in South Korea, Asia's second biggest fuel oil exporter to China after Singapore, are expected to peak in May and June, traders in Singapore said.
Similar maintenance shutdowns in Japan would also help boost market sentiment, they said.
While supplies would be reduced, import demand from China was expected to remain strong in May, estimated at over 500,000 tonnes, slightly more than in April.
Demand from Taiwan and India would also support prices, traders said. Taiwan has recently issued a tender to buy more than 400,000 tonnes of fuel between June and November.
Another bullish factor is that high freight costs have discouraged traders from moving Carribbean and United States fuel oil cargoes to Asia.
"A recovering high sulphur fuel oil market in Europe have closed the arbitrage window, limiting interest to bring cargoes to Asia," said one western trader in Asia.

High sulphur fuel oil prices in the benchmark Singapore spot market have risen by $1.00 per tonne two days ago to reach $97.50 per tonne on Thursday. Prices were above a $100 per tonned in late March.
